catalog_quote: Word stress is unpredictable and therefore phonemic. Stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable: kayu wood, baley house, makapala? thick. In a large number of words it falls on the final syllable, this being synchronically unpredictable: maheme full, mabaha? heavy, lumampa[ng] to walk. In other words stress falls on the third-last syllable: likudu? back, dakele? many. Stress contrast is shown by the following pairs: saha[ng] tree sp. and saha[ng] ant, mamuku (stem buku) to kneel and mamuku (stem puku) to bend, pahigi well and pahigi knife. In the present work stress in Ban is indicated wherever it does not fall on the penultimate syllable of the word.

A better, dedicated source exists (Utsumi 2010, 36 pp. on Bantik accent; also her 2005 PhD), not yet obtained and not found open. sources.quote: p.45: 'It has phonemic pitch accent, unlike its neighboring languages' (fn.1: 'pa'higi "well" and pahi'gi "knife" form a minimal pair'); 'Lexical stress is also important in Bantik.' Sec.2: proto-Sangiric penultimate stress (final if penult had schwa); schwa merger and paragogic vowel addition left stress in place, yielding minimal pairs (sa'hang 'palm leaf' vs saha'ng 'ant') and antepenultimate stress (ti'muhu?, da'tehe?, ka'para). fn.4 quotes Sneddon 1984 ('Stress is unpredictable and phonemic...') and adds: 'In my observation, however, many words have stress falling on the antepenultimate s
sources.locator: p.45 sec.1 and fn.1, sec.2 'Lexical phonemic stress and sentential intonation' with fn.4; pp.46-47 Figures 1-4 (F0 tracks of penultimate- vs final-stressed words)
sources.note: Modern first-hand statement with F0 tracks; explicitly endorses Sneddon's 'unpredictable and phonemic' and adds that antepenultimate stress is common; should be added as a corroborating citation on the record.
